questions.question: Can the Datadog Agent be installed and run on any operating system?
choices: No, it can only be installed on Linux distributions
No, you need to check that your operating system version is supported
Yes, any operating system and any version works without compatibility issues
Yes, as long as a system-wide Python 3 interpreter is available on the host
questions.explanation: Datadog publishes a Supported Platforms list with minimum versions per OS (for current Agent 7 releases, for example Ubuntu 14.04+, Windows Server 2016+ and macOS 12+), and older systems such as Windows Server 2012 R2 or CentOS/RHEL 6 are capped at older Agent releases. The Agent runs on Linux, Windows, macOS and containers, so it is not Linux-only, and it ships with its own embedded Python, so a host Python install is not what determines compatibility.

questions.question: You are installing the Datadog Agent on 10 hosts with a newly built Ansible control node. Ansible is set up, the hosts are in the inventory, and connectivity to them has been verified. What should you do NEXT on the Ansible control node?
choices: Run the Datadog one-line Agent install command on the control node
Set host_key_checking to False in the ansible.cfg file
Install the Datadog collection (or role) from Ansible Galaxy
Copy a prepared datadog.yaml file to every host in the inventory
questions.explanation: Datadog's Ansible docs say to install the Datadog content with the Ansible Galaxy CLI first (`ansible-galaxy collection install datadog.dd`), then reference the `datadog.dd.agent` role in a playbook with `datadog_api_key` and run it. Running the install command on the control node would only monitor the control node itself, host_key_checking is an SSH setting unrelated to Datadog (and connectivity already works), and datadog.yaml is generated by the role rather than copied by hand.

questions.question: Datadog provides official content for several configuration management (deployment) tools so you can install the Agent across many hosts. Which of the following is one of these tools?
choices: Kubernetes
Ansible
Red Hat Enterprise Linux
Docker
questions.explanation: Ansible is a configuration management and deployment tool; Datadog publishes the `datadog.dd` collection for it, alongside a Chef cookbook, a Puppet module and a SaltStack formula. Kubernetes is a container orchestrator (the Agent is deployed there with the Operator, Helm or a DaemonSet), Docker is a container runtime, and Red Hat Enterprise Linux is an operating system the Agent runs on.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the Datadog Agent?
choices: A cloud integration that polls provider APIs such as CloudWatch for host data
Software that runs on your hosts and sends their events and metrics to Datadog
A Datadog-hosted scanner that discovers and monitors hosts on your network remotely
A browser SDK that records user sessions and front-end performance in real time
questions.explanation: Datadog defines the Agent as software that runs on your hosts, collects events and metrics from them, and sends them to Datadog for analysis; it is also open source. Polling cloud provider APIs is what crawler-based integrations such as AWS do, Datadog does not remotely scan your network for hosts, and session recording is the job of the RUM browser SDK.

questions.question: Your organization uses the Datadog EU1 site (datadoghq.eu). Which command installs Agent 7 on an Ubuntu host and points it at the correct site?
choices: DD_API_KEY="<API_KEY>" DD_SITE="datadoghq.eu" bash -c "$(curl -L https://install.datadoghq.com/scripts/install_script_agent7.sh)"
DD_APP_KEY="<APP_KEY>" DD_SITE="datadoghq.eu" bash -c "$(curl -L https://install.datadoghq.com/scripts/install_script_agent7.sh)"
DD_API_KEY="<API_KEY>" DD_REGION="eu" bash -c "$(curl -L https://install.datadoghq.com/scripts/install_script_agent7.sh)"
sudo apt-get install datadog-agent --api-key="<API_KEY>" --site="datadoghq.eu"
questions.explanation: The install script reads the API key from `DD_API_KEY` (its only required variable) and the destination site from `DD_SITE`; without `DD_SITE` the Agent defaults to the US1 site datadoghq.com. Application keys are for API access rather than Agent intake, `DD_REGION` is not a variable the script uses, and apt-get has no Datadog-specific flags for keys or sites.

questions.question: When you run the Datadog Linux install script, which environment variable is required (unless you are upgrading from Agent 5)?
choices: DD_SITE
DD_HOSTNAME
DD_AGENT_MAJOR_VERSION
DD_API_KEY
questions.explanation: The install script documents that all variables are optional except `DD_API_KEY`, which ties the Agent's data to your organization. `DD_SITE` defaults to datadoghq.com, `DD_HOSTNAME` is only needed to force a specific hostname, and `DD_AGENT_MAJOR_VERSION` just selects Agent 6 or 7.

questions.question: You are baking a golden VM image and want the Linux install script to install the Agent package without starting the Agent. Which variable should you set?
choices: DD_UPGRADE
DD_INSTALL_ONLY
DD_AGENT_FLAVOR
DD_AGENT_MINOR_VERSION
questions.explanation: Setting `DD_INSTALL_ONLY` to any value prevents the script from starting the Agent after installation, which suits images and templates that are configured later. `DD_UPGRADE` triggers an upgrade from Agent 5, `DD_AGENT_FLAVOR` picks the binary type (such as datadog-iot-agent), and `DD_AGENT_MINOR_VERSION` pins a specific release.

questions.question: Which command performs a silent, unattended installation of the Windows Agent with your API key and site?
choices: msiexec /qn /i datadog-agent-7-latest.amd64.msi DD_API_KEY="<API_KEY>" DD_SITE="datadoghq.com"
msiexec /qn /i datadog-agent-7-latest.amd64.msi APIKEY="<API_KEY>" SITE="datadoghq.com"
agent.exe install --api-key "<API_KEY>" --site "datadoghq.com" --quiet
Install-Package datadog-agent -ApiKey "<API_KEY>" -Site "datadoghq.com"
questions.explanation: The Windows Agent ships as an MSI; `msiexec /qn /i` runs it quietly and the installer properties are `APIKEY` and `SITE` (others include TAGS, HOSTNAME and DDAGENTUSER_NAME), with Administrator rights required. `DD_API_KEY`/`DD_SITE` are the Linux script and container variable names, not MSI properties, and agent.exe has no install subcommand.

questions.question: After a default MSI installation on a Windows server, which account do the Datadog Agent services run as?
choices: dd-agent
LocalSystem
Administrator
ddagentuser
questions.explanation: The installer creates a `ddagentuser` account with a random password and runs the Agent services under it by default; you can choose another account with the DDAGENTUSER_NAME and DDAGENTUSER_PASSWORD MSI properties. `dd-agent` is the equivalent user on Linux, and LocalSystem is only an older, non-recommended configuration you can revert to manually.

questions.question: In the documented `docker run` command for the containerized Agent on Linux, why is `/var/run/docker.sock` mounted (read-only) into the container?
choices: So the Agent can query the Docker daemon for running containers and metadata
So the Agent can forward its metrics to Datadog through the Docker daemon
So the Agent can read the host's datadog.yaml through the Docker socket file
So the Agent can pull integration images from the Datadog container registry
questions.explanation: The Docker socket is the Docker Engine API, so mounting it lets the Agent discover containers, read their metadata and labels (used by Autodiscovery) and collect container metrics. The Agent sends data to Datadog directly over HTTPS through its Forwarder, not through the Docker daemon, and the containerized Agent is configured mainly with environment variables rather than a host datadog.yaml.

questions.question: The containerized Agent's `docker run` command also mounts the host's `/proc/` and `/sys/fs/cgroup/` as read-only volumes. What is the purpose of these mounts?
choices: To let the Agent write its log files and flares onto the host
To give the Agent permission to install packages on the host
To let the Agent read host and container resource statistics
To persist the Agent's configuration across container restarts
questions.explanation: `/proc` and the cgroup filesystem are where Linux exposes process, CPU, memory and I/O data for the host and for each container, so the Agent mounts them read-only (under /host) to report system and container metrics from inside its own container. Read-only mounts cannot be used to write logs, install packages or persist configuration; the containerized Agent is configured through environment variables.

questions.question: Datadog's Kubernetes installation docs list several ways to install the Agent. Which one is marked as the recommended method?
choices: The Datadog Operator
The Datadog Helm chart
A manually applied DaemonSet manifest
The Linux install script run on each node
questions.explanation: The Kubernetes installation docs list three methods: the Datadog Operator (recommended, and usable on OpenShift), Helm, and manual DaemonSet manifests. Helm and manual manifests are supported but not the recommended default, and running the host install script on nodes bypasses Kubernetes-native deployment entirely.

questions.question: In Kubernetes, which workload type runs the node-based Datadog Agent so that one Agent pod runs on every node?
choices: Deployment
StatefulSet
DaemonSet
CronJob
questions.explanation: Node-based Agents run as a DaemonSet, which schedules one pod per node and automatically adds a pod when a new node joins the cluster. A Deployment or StatefulSet runs a fixed number of replicas regardless of node count (the Cluster Agent runs as a Deployment), and a CronJob runs pods on a schedule rather than continuously.

questions.question: What is a key benefit of running the Datadog Cluster Agent alongside the node Agents in Kubernetes?
choices: It replaces the node Agents so only one Agent pod runs per cluster
It proxies the API server for node Agents, reducing load on it
It buffers every node's metrics on disk during Datadog outages
It collects host metrics from nodes that cannot run a DaemonSet
questions.explanation: The Cluster Agent sits between the Kubernetes API server and the node Agents, centralizing cluster-level collection (events, cluster checks, external metrics for HPA) while reducing API server load and the node Agents' RBAC needs. It complements rather than replaces the DaemonSet node Agents, which still collect each node's metrics; it is enabled by default with Helm chart v2.7.0+ and Operator v1.0.0+.

questions.question: Before deploying the Agent with the Datadog Operator, you need to store your API key in the cluster. Which command matches the documented approach?
choices: kubectl create secret generic datadog-secret --from-literal api-key=<DATADOG_API_KEY>
kubectl create configmap datadog-secret --from-literal api-key=<DATADOG_API_KEY>
helm install datadog-secret datadog/datadog --set-secret api-key=<DATADOG_API_KEY>
kubectl create secret docker-registry datadog-secret --docker-password=<DATADOG_API_KEY>
questions.explanation: The Kubernetes install docs create a generic secret with `kubectl create secret generic datadog-secret --from-literal api-key=<DATADOG_API_KEY>`, and the DatadogAgent resource (or Helm values) references it. A ConfigMap is not meant for credentials, a docker-registry secret stores image-pull credentials rather than an API key, and Helm has no `--set-secret` flag.

questions.question: With the Datadog Operator installed in your cluster, how do you tell it which Datadog components to deploy and how to configure them?
choices: Edit datadog.yaml on every node, then restart the kubelet
Pass a values file to the Operator with helm upgrade -f values.yaml
Add Datadog annotations to the kube-system namespace object
Apply a DatadogAgent custom resource with kubectl apply
questions.explanation: The Operator watches for a `DatadogAgent` custom resource: you describe the configuration (API key secret reference, cluster name, features) in a file such as datadog-agent.yaml and run `kubectl apply -f datadog-agent.yaml`. A values.yaml passed to Helm configures the Helm chart method (or the Operator's own install), not the Agent deployment the Operator manages, and nodes do not get a hand-edited datadog.yaml.

questions.question: Your team deploys software with Chef. Using Datadog's `datadog` cookbook, which recipe installs and configures the Agent on a node?
choices: datadog::dd-handler
datadog::agent-install
datadog::dd-agent
datadog::default-agent
questions.explanation: The Chef cookbook, published on Chef Supermarket, provides `datadog::dd-agent` to install and configure the Agent, with the API key set through `node['datadog']['api_key']`. `datadog::dd-handler` is the other main recipe, but it reports Chef run details to Datadog rather than installing the Agent; the remaining names are not cookbook recipes.

questions.question: Which command installs Datadog's Puppet module so you can deploy the Agent with Puppet?
choices: puppet module install datadog-datadog_agent
ansible-galaxy collection install datadog.dd
knife cookbook site install datadog
puppet agent --install datadog-agent
questions.explanation: Datadog's module is published on Puppet Forge as `datadog-datadog_agent` and installed with `puppet module install`; you then declare `class { 'datadog_agent': api_key => ... }` in a manifest. The ansible-galaxy and knife commands install Datadog's Ansible collection and Chef cookbook respectively, and `puppet agent` runs the Puppet client rather than installing modules.

questions.question: What is a key difference between Datadog Agent v7 and Agent v6?
choices: Agent v7 runs only Python 3 checks; v6 can still run Python 2
Agent v7 drops DogStatsD, so it must now be installed separately
Agent v7 runs only in containers; Agent v6 is needed on bare metal
Agent v7 needs an application key in addition to an API key to run
questions.explanation: Agent 7 only supports Python 3 custom checks, while Agent v6 embeds Python 2 (and from v6.14 can optionally enable a Python 3 runtime). Both versions include DogStatsD, run on hosts as well as containers, and need only an API key to submit data; application keys are for API access.

questions.question: Your Agent v6 hosts run several custom checks written for Python 2, and you plan to upgrade them to Agent v7. What should you do first?
choices: Set DD_UPGRADE so the install script converts the checks
Nothing; Agent v7 runs Python 2 checks in a legacy mode
Verify the custom checks are compatible with Python 3
Delete conf.d so Agent v7 can regenerate its check configs
questions.explanation: The upgrade guide says to verify that your custom checks are Python 3 compatible before upgrading, because Agent 7 only supports Python 3 custom checks and the upgrade does not migrate them for you. `DD_UPGRADE` is for upgrading from Agent 5, not for converting code, and deleting conf.d would simply remove your check configurations.

questions.question: Your EC2 instances already appear in Datadog through the AWS integration. What is a main reason to also install the Datadog Agent on them?
choices: The Agent collects far more metrics at 15-second resolution
The AWS integration stops reporting instances that have no Agent
CloudWatch can only report EC2 CPU usage when an Agent is present
The Agent lets CloudWatch poll each instance at one-second resolution
questions.explanation: Cloud providers sample hosts externally (AWS exposes per-minute metrics through its API), whereas the Agent collects performance statistics every 15 seconds, enables 50+ metrics by default, and adds integrations, logs, APM and process data. The AWS integration keeps reporting instances without an Agent, and installing the Agent does not change how CloudWatch itself collects data.

questions.question: An EC2 instance is discovered by the AWS integration and also runs the Datadog Agent. How is this instance counted for infrastructure host billing?
choices: Twice: once for the integration and once for the Agent
Not at all, because Agent hosts are billed as custom metrics
Only by the integration, because it discovered the host first
Once: you are not billed twice for the same instance
questions.explanation: Datadog's AWS billing docs state that you are not billed twice if you run the Agent on an EC2 instance picked up by the AWS integration; the two sources are reconciled into one host. For IMDSv2 instances this matching requires Agent 7.64.0+ or `ec2_prefer_imdsv2: true`, otherwise the Agent cannot report the instance ID and the host may be double-counted.

questions.question: A customer wants to install the newest Agent 7 release on hosts running Windows Server 2012 R2. What should you tell them?
choices: Support for this OS ends at Agent 7.46.0, so pin an older version
Any Agent 7 release works, since every Windows Server is supported
Windows needs Agent v5, because Agents 6 and 7 are Linux-only
They must run the Agent in a Linux container on the Windows host
questions.explanation: The Supported Platforms page caps Windows Server 2012 and 2012 R2 at Agent 6 versions up to 6.46.0 and Agent 7 versions up to 7.46.0, and the current v7 list starts at Windows Server 2016, which is why you should always check OS version compatibility first. Agents 6 and 7 fully support Windows, and running a Linux container is not the documented workaround.

questions.question: The Datadog Agent on an Ubuntu host was stopped so that a configuration file could be edited. The edit is complete. Which command starts the Agent again?
choices: sudo datadog-agent restart
sudo service datadog-agent restart
sudo service datadog-agent start
sudo datadog-agent start-service
questions.explanation: The Agent is already stopped, so the service manager's start action is the right command: `sudo service datadog-agent start` (equivalent to `sudo systemctl start datadog-agent` on systemd). `restart` is used when you change configuration while the Agent is running, `datadog-agent restart` is not an Agent subcommand, and `start-service` is a Windows-only subcommand.

questions.question: On a systemd-based Linux host, which command restarts the Agent service as shown in Datadog's Linux documentation?
choices: sudo systemctl restart dd-agent
sudo systemctl restart datadog-agent
sudo datadog-agent restart-service
sudo launchctl kickstart -k system/com.datadoghq.agent
questions.explanation: The Linux commands table uses `sudo systemctl restart datadog-agent`, because the service unit is named datadog-agent. `dd-agent` is the Linux user account the Agent runs as, not the unit name, `restart-service` is a Windows-only subcommand, and launchctl is the macOS service manager.

questions.question: You manage a legacy upstart-based host (CentOS/RHEL 6) running a supported Agent version. How should you adapt the documented `sudo systemctl stop datadog-agent` command?
choices: Use `sudo stop datadog-agent`, swapping `systemctl <action>` for `<action>`
Use `sudo launchctl stop datadog-agent`, since upstart wraps launchd
Use `sudo datadog-agent stopservice`, the cross-platform stop command
Use `sudo systemctl --upstart stop datadog-agent` to pick the init system
questions.explanation: Datadog's Linux docs note that on upstart-based systems such as CentOS/RHEL 6 or SUSE 11 you swap `systemctl <action>` with `<action>`, giving `sudo stop datadog-agent`, `sudo start datadog-agent` and so on. launchctl is macOS-only, `stopservice` is a Windows-only subcommand, and systemctl has no --upstart option. Note that Agent support for CentOS/RHEL 6 ends at 7.51.1.

questions.question: Which agent.exe subcommand restarts the Windows Agent within the Windows service control manager?
choices: stopservice
launch-gui
restart-service
start-service
questions.explanation: `restart-service` restarts the Agent within the service control manager and, like `start-service` and `stopservice`, is Windows-only; run it from an elevated prompt, for example `& "$env:ProgramFiles\Datadog\Datadog Agent\bin\agent.exe" restart-service`. `stopservice` only stops the service, `start-service` only starts it, and `launch-gui` opens the Datadog Agent Manager.

questions.question: A Windows administrator wants to restart the Agent with PowerShell's `Restart-Service` cmdlet. Which service name should they pass?
choices: datadog-agent
dd-agent
ddagentuser
datadogagent
questions.explanation: The Windows service is named DatadogAgent (display name 'Datadog Agent'); Datadog's docs use `restart-service -f datadogagent`, where -Force is needed because the trace and process Agent services depend on it. services.msc also works. `datadog-agent` is the Linux service unit name, `dd-agent` is the Linux user account, and `ddagentuser` is the Windows account the service runs as, not the service itself.

questions.question: A developer installed the Agent on a macOS workstation and wants to restart it from the terminal. Which command follows the documented macOS approach?
choices: sudo systemctl restart system/com.datadoghq.agent.service
sudo launchctl kickstart -k system/com.datadoghq.agent
sudo service datadog-agent restart --macos
sudo datadog-agent restart-service --launchd
questions.explanation: macOS services are managed by launchd, so the macOS page uses launchctl: `sudo launchctl kickstart -k system/com.datadoghq.agent` restarts the Agent (kickstart without -k starts it, and `kill SIGTERM` stops it). systemctl and service are Linux service managers and `restart-service` is Windows-only; on macOS you can also manage the Agent from the web GUI or systray app.

questions.question: You started the containerized Agent with `docker run -d --name dd-agent ... -e DD_API_KEY=<KEY> registry.datadoghq.com/agent:7` and now need to add `-e DD_LOGS_ENABLED=true`. What must you do?
choices: Run `docker restart dd-agent` so it rereads its environment
Edit /etc/datadog-agent/datadog.yaml on the host and reboot
Remove the container and re-run docker run with the new variable
Run `docker exec dd-agent agent restart-service` to reload settings
questions.explanation: A container's environment variables are fixed when it is created, which is why the Agent Commands page says to start or restart the Docker Agent with the installation command: remove the old container and run `docker run` again with the added variable. `docker restart` keeps the original environment, `restart-service` is Windows-only, and the containerized Agent does not read a host datadog.yaml unless you explicitly mount one.

questions.question: How do you restart a node Agent pod that runs as part of the Datadog DaemonSet in Kubernetes?
choices: Delete the Agent pod; the DaemonSet recreates it automatically
Run `sudo systemctl restart datadog-agent` on the node
Run `kubectl exec <POD> -- agent restart-service` in the pod
Scale the Cluster Agent Deployment down to zero and back to one
questions.explanation: The Agent Commands page documents `kubectl delete pod <AGENT POD NAME>` for stopping and restarting on Kubernetes, because the DaemonSet controller automatically reschedules a fresh pod on that node. There is no systemd-managed Agent on the node, `restart-service` is Windows-only, and the Cluster Agent is a separate component whose restart does not restart node Agents.

questions.question: By default, how often does the Agent's Collector gather standard metrics?
choices: Every 60 seconds
Every 5 minutes
Every 1 second
Every 15 seconds
questions.explanation: The Agent architecture page states that the collector gathers all standard metrics every 15 seconds, a much finer resolution than cloud provider APIs offer. Minute-level or multi-minute intervals are typical of cloud provider polling (AWS exposes per-minute metrics), and the Agent does not collect every second by default.

questions.question: In Agent v6 and v7, which two components make up the main Agent process?
choices: The Trace Agent and the Process Agent
The Cluster Agent and the node Agent
The Collector and the Forwarder
The System Probe and the Security Agent
questions.explanation: The main Agent process is made up of the Collector, which runs checks and collects metrics, and the Forwarder, which sends payloads to Datadog; DogStatsD also runs inside it. The Trace (APM) Agent and Process Agent are separate optional processes, as are the System Probe and Security Agent, and the Cluster Agent is a Kubernetes-specific component.

questions.question: The network link between a host and Datadog drops for a few minutes. How does the Agent's Forwarder handle metrics during the outage?
choices: It stops the Collector until the connection to Datadog comes back
It buffers them in memory, dropping the oldest past a limit
It writes them to datadog.yaml so they can be uploaded later
It routes them through DogStatsD over UDP to a nearby Agent
questions.explanation: The Forwarder buffers metrics in memory so network splits don't affect reporting; once a size or outstanding-request limit is reached, the oldest metrics are discarded to keep its memory footprint manageable. The Collector keeps running checks during the outage, datadog.yaml is a configuration file rather than a data store, and DogStatsD receives metrics from local applications instead of relaying them to other Agents.

questions.question: With a default Agent v7 installation, which statement about the APM (trace) Agent and the Process Agent is accurate?
choices: APM Agent is disabled; Process Agent collects all live processes
Both are disabled until you enable them in datadog.yaml
Both are enabled and collect traces and all live processes
APM Agent is enabled; Process Agent only collects container data
questions.explanation: The architecture page describes the APM Agent as enabled by default, while the Process Agent is disabled by default except for container collection, so live process collection must be turned on explicitly. That rules out both the 'both disabled' and the 'both fully enabled' descriptions, as well as a disabled APM Agent.

questions.question: On which platforms is the Agent's browser-based GUI (the Datadog Agent Manager) enabled by default?
choices: Linux only
Windows and macOS
Linux and Windows
All platforms, including containers
questions.explanation: The GUI runs on port 5002 by default on Windows and macOS and is disabled by default on Linux, where you must configure a GUI port to use it; setting the port to -1 disables it anywhere. You open it with `datadog-agent launch-gui` (`agent.exe launch-gui` on Windows), so any option that includes Linux by default is wrong.

questions.question: A colleague tries to open the Agent GUI of a Windows server by browsing to http://<server-ip>:5002 from their laptop, but it does not load. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The GUI requires an application key to be entered in the browser
The GUI listens on port 8126, which is shared with the Trace Agent
The GUI only accepts connections from localhost on the Agent host
The GUI is only reachable through the Datadog web app's host view
questions.explanation: For security, the Agent GUI can only be accessed from the local network interface (localhost/127.0.0.1), so you must be on the host running the Agent, and the browser must have cookies enabled. It does not use application keys, it listens on port 5002 by default (8126 is the APM port), and it is not exposed through the Datadog web app.

questions.question: The Linux docs run checks with `sudo -u dd-agent -- datadog-agent check <CHECK_NAME>` rather than as root. Why run the check as the dd-agent user?
choices: It runs the check with the Agent service's own permissions
Only the dd-agent user is allowed to send data to Datadog
Running checks as root would overwrite the check's conf.yaml
The check subcommand refuses to run from an interactive shell
questions.explanation: On Linux the Agent service runs as the unprivileged `dd-agent` user, so running a check as that user reproduces the permissions the real Agent has (for example, whether it can read a log file or socket); root might succeed where the service fails. Data submission is authorized by the API key, not the OS user, root does not overwrite configs, and the check subcommand works fine from a shell.

questions.question: You edit an integration's conf.yaml under /etc/datadog-agent/conf.d/ on a Linux host. What must you do for the change to take effect?
choices: Nothing; the Agent re-reads its config files every 15 seconds
Restart the Agent
Run `datadog-agent configcheck` to apply the new configuration
Reinstall the Agent package so the new file is registered
questions.explanation: Configuration changes are picked up when the Agent restarts, so Datadog's guides tell you to run the restart command (for example `sudo service datadog-agent restart` on Ubuntu); the Windows docs likewise say the service must be restarted whenever you modify an integration. The 15-second interval is for metric collection, not config reloading, `configcheck` only prints configurations already loaded, and reinstalling is unnecessary.

questions.question: On Linux, what is the difference between `sudo systemctl status datadog-agent` and `sudo datadog-agent status`?
choices: The first shows check results; the second shows only whether it is running
They are identical; the second one is simply an alias for the first command
The first works only in containers; the second only works on bare-metal hosts
The first shows the service state; the second shows the Agent's status page
questions.explanation: The Linux commands table lists `systemctl status datadog-agent` as the status of the Agent service (running or not, as systemd sees it) and `datadog-agent status` as the status page of the running Agent, which details checks, forwarder activity, hostnames and errors. They are not aliases, and both are host commands; in containers you run `agent status` through docker exec or kubectl exec.

questions.question: You run `sudo apt-get remove datadog-agent -y` on an Ubuntu host. According to Datadog's docs, which of the following is left behind on the host?
choices: The running Agent service, which keeps sending metrics
The datadog.yaml file and the dd-agent user account
The Agent package, disabled but still marked installed
Nothing; apt-get remove deletes every Agent file and user
questions.explanation: The Linux uninstall docs warn that the remove commands delete the Agent but not the datadog.yaml configuration file, user-created files in the configuration folders, the dd-agent user, or Datadog log files; a separate cleanup command removes those. Removing the package uninstalls the service itself, so it is neither still running nor still installed.

questions.question: The Agent is installed with default settings on an Amazon EC2 instance that still has its default EC2 hostname (for example ip-172-31-5-10), and no hostname is set in datadog.yaml. Which name does the Agent report as the host's canonical hostname?
choices: None; on AWS the hostname must be set in datadog.yaml
The instance's private IP address, such as 172.31.5.10
The EC2 instance ID, read from the EC2 metadata endpoint
The value of the instance's Name tag in the EC2 console
questions.explanation: When no hostname is configured and the DNS/OS hostname is an EC2 default like ip-172-31-5-10, the Agent uses the instance ID (i-...) as long as it can reach the EC2 metadata endpoint. The instance ID is not used unconditionally: a meaningful, non-default hostname would win. A configured hostname is never mandatory on AWS, IP addresses are not hostname candidates, and the Name tag is reported as metadata (aws_name) rather than as the canonical hostname.

questions.question: When the Agent chooses its canonical hostname, which candidate is evaluated first?
choices: The EC2 instance ID from instance metadata
The DNS hostname of the machine
A hostname set in the Agent config file
The host's primary IP address
questions.explanation: The hostname rules are applied in order and the first match wins: a hostname configured for the Agent (the datadog.yaml `hostname` option, or DD_HOSTNAME), then a DNS hostname that is not an EC2 default, then the EC2 instance ID, then the DNS hostname as a fallback. The host's IP address is not one of the candidate names.

questions.question: On an EC2 instance you set `hostname: ip-10-1-2-3` in datadog.yaml and restart the Agent, but Datadog still shows the host under its instance ID. What explains this?
choices: Configured hostnames are always ignored on EC2 while the AWS integration is enabled
Configured names starting with ip- or domu are skipped unless forced as canonical
The hostname option only applies after the old host is deleted in the Infrastructure List
The datadog.yaml hostname option is ignored; only the DD_HOSTNAME variable works
questions.explanation: A configured hostname is used only if it does not start with ip- or domu (EC2 default patterns); otherwise that rule is skipped and the Agent falls through to the instance ID. Since Agent 6.16/7.16, setting `hostname_force_config_as_canonical: true` accepts such a name (existing hosts may need Datadog support to rename them in-app). The AWS integration does not disable configured hostnames, and the datadog.yaml `hostname` option is fully supported.

questions.question: An on-premises Linux server's FQDN is web-01.corp.example.com, but with Agent v7 defaults it shows up in Datadog as web-01. Which datadog.yaml setting makes the Agent report the fully qualified name?
choices: hostname_force_config_as_canonical: true
hostname_fqdn: true
ec2_prefer_imdsv2: true
ec2_use_windows_prefix_detection: true
questions.explanation: Agent v6 and later on Linux use Go's `os.Hostname()` rather than `hostname -f`, which can yield the short name; enabling `hostname_fqdn` (available since v6.3 and disabled by default) restores FQDN reporting. `hostname_force_config_as_canonical` concerns configured ip-/domu names, and the two ec2_ options only affect how EC2 metadata and Windows EC2 default hostnames are handled.

questions.question: Which command prints the hostname that the Datadog Agent is actually using?
choices: hostname -f
sudo datadog-agent hostname
sudo datadog-agent configcheck
sudo datadog-agent diagnose
questions.explanation: The `hostname` subcommand prints the hostname used by the Agent, and the `status` output also lists the hostname candidates it detected. `hostname -f` shows the operating system's FQDN, which can differ from the Agent's choice (for example on EC2 or with hostname_fqdn disabled), `configcheck` prints loaded check configurations, and `diagnose` runs connectivity diagnostics.

questions.question: An EC2 host has the instance ID i-abcd1234, the EC2 default hostname ip-192-0-0-1, and the DNS name myhost.mydomain from an internal DNS server. How does Datadog represent this host?
choices: As three separate hosts, one for each of the identifying names
As one canonical hostname, with the others kept as aliases
As one host named i-abcd1234; the other two names are discarded
As one host whose name joins all three values with hyphens
questions.explanation: Datadog creates host aliases when a single host has multiple uniquely identifiable names: the Agent chooses one canonical hostname using its resolution rules and reports the other names it collected as aliases. This avoids duplicate hosts and lets data from the AWS integration, which knows the instance ID, map to the same host instead of being discarded or split.

questions.question: An engineer searches the Infrastructure List for a host by one of its aliases (an older DNS name) and gets no result, even though the host is reporting. Why?
choices: Aliases expire 15 minutes after the Agent last restarted on the host
Aliases are visible only in the output of the datadog-agent status command
Aliases are created only for hosts that do not run the Datadog Agent
Aliases are shown only in the host's inspect panel and cannot be searched
questions.explanation: Host aliases are displayed in the inspect (detail) panel of the Infrastructure List but are not available for searching or filtering, so you must search by the canonical hostname. Aliases do not expire on Agent restarts, they are collected by the Agent itself rather than only for Agent-less hosts, and they are visible in the Datadog UI rather than only in local command output.

questions.question: You change the `hostname` value in datadog.yaml on a host and restart the Agent. What happens to the old hostname in Datadog?
choices: It is merged into the new hostname at once, along with its full metric history
It keeps receiving the host's metrics as an alias of the new hostname
It stays listed for two hours without new data; old data is still queryable
It is deleted immediately along with every metric it previously reported
questions.explanation: Datadog's tagging docs note that after a hostname change the old hostname remains in the UI for two hours but does not show new metrics, and its data can still be queried through the API; to see both in one graph you combine the two metrics with arithmetic. History is not merged automatically, the old name does not keep receiving data, and past data is not deleted.

questions.question: In an EKS cluster, each worker node appears twice in the Infrastructure List: once under the name reported by the Agent and once under the EC2 instance ID from the AWS integration. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The Agent pods cannot reach EC2 metadata, so no instance ID alias is sent
The AWS integration and the Agent are configured with different API keys
The Cluster Agent reports every node a second time using its instance ID
The node Agents are sending data to two different Datadog sites at once
questions.explanation: The Agent normally queries the EC2 Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) and submits the instance ID as a hostname alias so Datadog can merge its data with the AWS integration's host. If the Agent pods cannot reach IMDS (for example IMDSv2 with a hop limit of 1, or an Agent older than 7.64.0 without DD_EC2_PREFER_IMDSV2), the alias is missing and duplicates appear, so the fix is to allow metadata access. API keys, the Cluster Agent and site selection do not produce this pattern.

questions.question: A containerized Agent on a CI runner exits with the error "unable to reliably determine the host name". What is the most direct fix?
choices: Set DD_SITE so the Agent can look up its hostname from Datadog
Set the DD_HOSTNAME environment variable on the Agent container
Mount the host's /etc/hostname file over /var/run/docker.sock
Add hostname_fqdn: true to the datadog.yaml file on the runner
questions.explanation: The containerized Agent tries the kubelet, cloud provider metadata and the container runtime to find a hostname; when none of them works it fails with this error, and Datadog's fix is to set the hostname explicitly, for example `-e DD_HOSTNAME=$(hostname)`. DD_SITE only selects the intake site, mounting a file over the Docker socket path would break access to the container runtime API (itself a hostname source), and hostname_fqdn only changes the form of a hostname that was already found.

questions.question: When installing the Windows Agent with msiexec, which installer property overrides the hostname the Agent reports?
choices: HOSTNAME_FQDN_ENABLED
DDAGENTUSER_NAME
HOSTNAME
TAGS
questions.explanation: The `HOSTNAME` MSI property sets the hostname the Agent reports, overriding the name it would otherwise calculate at runtime. `HOSTNAME_FQDN_ENABLED` only makes the Agent use the FQDN form of the detected name, `DDAGENTUSER_NAME` sets the Windows service account, and `TAGS` assigns host tags.

questions.question: Your EC2 instances enforce IMDSv2, and those running Agent 7.50 appear as duplicate hosts and are counted twice. Which documented change fixes this?
choices: Set hostname_fqdn to true in datadog.yaml on every instance
Add the same host tags in the AWS integration and datadog.yaml
Set each instance's EC2 Name tag to match its Agent hostname
Upgrade to Agent 7.64.0+ or set ec2_prefer_imdsv2 to true
questions.explanation: To avoid double counting, the Agent must read the instance ID from instance metadata and report it so Datadog can reconcile the Agent host with the AWS integration's host. Agent 7.64.0 and later use IMDSv2 by default, while older versions need `ec2_prefer_imdsv2: true` (DD_EC2_PREFER_IMDSV2 in containers). FQDN reporting, matching host tags or Name tags do not give Datadog the instance ID it uses for matching.

questions.question: If the Agent runs in a containerized environment and cannot determine a reliable hostname automatically, which configuration can explicitly set it?
choices: DD_API_KEY
DD_HOSTNAME
DD_DOGSTATSD_PORT
DD_PROCESS_AGENT_ENABLED
questions.explanation: DD_HOSTNAME lets you explicitly control the hostname the Agent reports. That is useful when automatic hostname detection is unavailable or unreliable in certain containerized environments.

questions.question: For a basic host-based Agent install, which two values are required so the Agent can send data to the correct Datadog organization and site?
choices: Monitor ID and dashboard ID
API key and site
Hostname and log path
Application key and password
questions.explanation: The Agent's main required settings are your organization's API key and the Datadog site value. The API key authorizes intake, and the site tells the Agent which Datadog region or domain to send data to.

questions.question: If hostname autodetection fails in a containerized environment, which explicit setting can be used as a fallback?
choices: DD_HOSTNAME
DD_TAGS
DD_API_KEY
DD_SITE
questions.explanation: Datadog documents `DD_HOSTNAME` as a way to explicitly set the hostname when autodetection is not reliable. That can be important in containers, CI environments, or sidecar patterns where the Agent cannot infer a trustworthy host identity.

questions.question: A single machine starts appearing as two slightly different hosts in Datadog over time. Which area should you investigate first?
choices: Dashboard color palettes
Hostname detection and any explicit Agent hostname overrides
The browser used to view the Host Map
DogStatsD sample rate defaults
questions.explanation: Duplicate or drifting host identities usually point to hostname detection, cloud metadata, or explicit hostname settings. That is the right layer to inspect before looking at dashboards or visualizations.

questions.question: On Kubernetes, which method is Datadog's recommended way to install and configure the Agent and its integrations declaratively?
choices: Copying datadog.yaml into each pod manually
Running dogstatsd inside every application container
Installing the Agent through the host package manager only
Using the Datadog Helm chart or the Datadog Operator
questions.explanation: Datadog provides a Helm chart and a Datadog Operator for installing the Agent on Kubernetes. Both declare the Agent, Cluster Agent, and collection settings as Kubernetes resources so configuration is reproducible and versionable.

questions.question: Why does an operating system hostname matter to monitoring tools such as Datadog?
choices: It helps identify and group telemetry from the correct host
It sets the CPU clock speed
It changes UDP traffic into TCP traffic
It determines disk encryption type
questions.explanation: A hostname gives Datadog a stable way to associate incoming telemetry with a specific machine or node. Without a reliable host identity, dashboards, maps, and correlations can become misleading or incomplete.

questions.question: After installing the Agent on a Linux host, what is the best first check to confirm integrations are running cleanly?
choices: Create a dashboard immediately
Run the Agent status command
Open more inbound firewall ports
Revoke the API key
questions.explanation: The Agent status output shows running checks, warnings, and integration health. Datadog's troubleshooting guidance points to the status command early because it exposes whether the Agent and integrations are actually working on the host.

questions.question: After editing datadog.yaml or an integration conf.yaml, what usually must happen before the new settings take effect?
choices: Rotate the API key
Rebuild the Datadog web UI
Restart the Agent
Delete all old host tags
questions.explanation: Agent-side configuration changes are typically loaded when the Agent starts. Restarting ensures the process re-reads the updated files and applies the new settings.

questions.question: Why is the Datadog Agent typically installed to run as a service or daemon rather than launched from an interactive shell?
choices: So the Agent can use application keys instead of API keys
So integration files are stored only in memory
So collection continues after the user logs out and the host reboots
So dashboards update without network connectivity
questions.explanation: A service or daemon can keep running independently of an interactive login session. That lets the Agent start at boot and continue collecting telemetry even after a user disconnects.

questions.question: Why is a stable hostname important for Datadog host monitoring?
choices: It replaces the need for API keys
It encrypts logs automatically
It helps Datadog associate telemetry with the correct host over time
It increases CPU speed on the host
questions.explanation: A stable hostname helps Datadog recognize that data belongs to the same machine across time and across products. If host identity changes unexpectedly, visibility can fragment or duplicate host entries can appear.

questions.question: Cloned virtual machines all appear under the same host in Datadog after the Agent starts. Which action most directly fixes the identity problem?
choices: Replace the API key with an application key
Explicitly set a unique Agent hostname on each machine
Lower the DogStatsD flush interval
Change the dashboard rollup function
questions.explanation: Datadog uses host identity to merge telemetry correctly. If cloned machines share the same detected name, explicitly setting unique hostnames prevents collisions.

questions.question: Why should the Datadog Agent have a stable, correct hostname?
choices: To compress logs before shipping them
To increase CPU speed on the monitored host
To rotate API keys automatically
To associate telemetry with the correct infrastructure entity in Datadog
questions.explanation: The Agent hostname is a key part of how Datadog identifies hosts and joins related data together. If that hostname is wrong or unstable, metrics and metadata can be split across multiple apparent hosts or attached to the wrong one.

questions.question: If you explicitly change the Agent hostname in datadog.yaml, what is true in Datadog?
choices: The new hostname is ignored until you create a new organization
Both old and new hostnames permanently receive the same new metrics
The old hostname can remain visible for about two hours, but new metrics arrive under the new hostname
The old hostname immediately disappears from the UI and its historical data is deleted
questions.explanation: Datadog keeps the previous hostname visible for a short period so recent history does not vanish abruptly. New telemetry is attributed to the newly configured hostname, while the old name stops receiving fresh metrics.

questions.question: Why is the Datadog Agent typically installed as a background service or daemon on a host?
choices: It converts all TCP traffic on the host into UDP traffic
It can continuously collect and forward telemetry without an interactive session
It is required to compile dashboards locally on the host
It can only run while an interactive user is logged in
questions.explanation: The Agent is designed to run continuously so it can keep collecting metrics, events, logs, and traces as the host operates. Running it as a service or daemon means monitoring continues through reboots and user logouts.

questions.question: After installing or changing an Agent integration package, what action is typically required before new data starts flowing?
choices: Restart the Agent
Clear the browser cache
Rotate the API key immediately
Change the host's timezone
questions.explanation: Integration installs and configuration changes generally require the Agent to reload or restart so the new check can initialize cleanly. Without that step, the running process may continue using the old configuration state.

questions.question: In Kubernetes, the Agent exits soon after startup with an error saying it was unable to reliably determine the host name. What is the best interpretation?
choices: A dashboard permission is missing
DogStatsD has a port conflict on localhost
Hostname resolution failed, so the Agent cannot safely identify the host
An application key is missing for metric intake
questions.explanation: Datadog documents this as a hostname detection problem in containerized environments, not as a dashboard or API-key issue. The Agent depends on a reliable host identity, so it may exit rather than send ambiguous host telemetry.

questions.question: What is the role of the Datadog Cluster Agent in a Kubernetes deployment?
choices: It replaces the Node Agents entirely
It collects host metrics directly from the kernel
It acts as a control-plane component that aggregates cluster metadata and serves Autodiscovery and cluster-level checks to Node Agents
It forwards DogStatsD traffic to Datadog over UDP port 53
questions.explanation: The Cluster Agent runs as a Kubernetes deployment and provides cluster-wide context such as pod metadata, service-to-service mapping, and cluster-level checks. Node Agents communicate with the Cluster Agent to enrich host-level telemetry and coordinate Autodiscovery.

questions.question: For Datadog Agent v6+, how can most settings from datadog.yaml also be supplied in containerized deployments?
choices: Through browser local storage
Through dashboard template variables
Through DD_ environment variables
Through monitor tags
questions.explanation: The Agent supports environment-variable forms for most main configuration settings, typically by uppercasing the option name and prefixing it with DD_. This is especially common in containers where editing files directly is less convenient.

flashcards.front: What is the Datadog Agent?
flashcards.back: Open-source software that runs on your hosts, collects events and metrics (plus logs, traces and processes when enabled) and sends them to Datadog. Agent v7 is the current major version.

flashcards.front: Agent v7 supported platforms (high level)
flashcards.back:
Linux x86_64 and ARM64 (x86_64 minimums, e.g. Ubuntu 14.04+, Debian 8+, RHEL/CentOS 7+, Amazon Linux 2/2023), Windows Server 2016+ and Windows 10/11, macOS 12+ (current releases), Docker 1.14+, Kubernetes 1.3+.
Always check the Supported Platforms list for your OS version; unlisted OSes may work with a source install.

flashcards.front: Which older operating systems are capped at older Agent releases?
flashcards.back:
Windows Server 2012 / 2012 R2: Agent 6 <= 6.46.0 and Agent 7 <= 7.46.0
CentOS/RHEL 6: Agent 6 <= 6.51.1 and Agent 7 <= 7.51.1
macOS (x86): 10.14 up to Agent 7.61.0; 11 up to Agent 7.74.1

flashcards.front: Linux one-line install command for Agent 7
flashcards.back:
DD_API_KEY="<API_KEY>" DD_SITE="<SITE>" bash -c "$(curl -L https://install.datadoghq.com/scripts/install_script_agent7.sh)"
Fleet Automation's in-app install page generates this with your key pre-filled.

flashcards.front: Key Linux install script environment variables
flashcards.back:
DD_API_KEY: required (unless DD_UPGRADE)
DD_SITE: intake site (default datadoghq.com)
DD_AGENT_MAJOR_VERSION / DD_AGENT_MINOR_VERSION: version pinning
DD_HOSTNAME: force the hostname
DD_INSTALL_ONLY: install without starting the Agent
DD_UPGRADE: upgrade from Agent 5

flashcards.front: Silent Windows Agent install command and common MSI properties
flashcards.back:
msiexec /qn /i datadog-agent-7-latest.amd64.msi APIKEY="<API_KEY>" SITE="datadoghq.com" (run as Administrator)
Other properties: TAGS, HOSTNAME, HOSTNAME_FQDN_ENABLED, DDAGENTUSER_NAME / DDAGENTUSER_PASSWORD, LOGS_ENABLED, APM_ENABLED, PROCESS_ENABLED, PROXY_HOST / PROXY_PORT.

flashcards.front: How is the Agent installed on macOS?
flashcards.back:
With the install script generated in Fleet Automation, e.g. DD_API_KEY="<API_KEY>" DD_SITE="<SITE>" bash -c "$(curl -L https://install.datadoghq.com/scripts/install_mac_os.sh)"
The Agent installs under /opt/datadog-agent and runs as a launchd service (com.datadoghq.agent). Current Agent 7 releases require macOS 12+.

flashcards.front: Docker Agent install command (Linux) and its mounts
flashcards.back:
docker run -d --cgroupns host --pid host --name dd-agent -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro -v /proc/:/host/proc/:ro -v /sys/fs/cgroup/:/host/sys/fs/cgroup:ro -e DD_SITE=<DATADOG_SITE> -e DD_API_KEY=<DATADOG_API_KEY> registry.datadoghq.com/agent:7
docker.sock: talk to the Docker daemon (containers, metadata); /proc and cgroup: host and container resource metrics. DD_API_KEY is required.

flashcards.front: Kubernetes installation methods for the Agent
flashcards.back:
1. Datadog Operator (recommended; also OpenShift): helm install datadog-operator datadog/datadog-operator, then kubectl apply -f datadog-agent.yaml (a DatadogAgent resource)
2. Helm chart: helm install <RELEASE_NAME> -f datadog-values.yaml datadog/datadog
3. Manual DaemonSet manifests
The API key goes in a secret: kubectl create secret generic datadog-secret --from-literal api-key=<DATADOG_API_KEY>

flashcards.front: Datadog Cluster Agent
flashcards.back: A centralized Kubernetes component that proxies the API server for the node Agents (a DaemonSet), reducing API server load and node RBAC needs. It collects cluster-level data and events, runs cluster checks, and serves external metrics for HPA. Enabled by default with Helm chart v2.7.0+ and Operator v1.0.0+.

flashcards.front: Installing the Agent with Ansible
flashcards.back:
1. On the control node: ansible-galaxy collection install datadog.dd (Ansible 2.10+; Windows targets also need ansible.windows)
2. In a playbook, import the role datadog.dd.agent and set datadog_api_key
3. Run the playbook against your inventory

flashcards.front: Datadog content for Chef, Puppet and SaltStack
flashcards.back:
Chef: 'datadog' cookbook on Chef Supermarket; recipe datadog::dd-agent installs the Agent (datadog::dd-handler reports Chef runs)
Puppet: datadog-datadog_agent module on Puppet Forge (puppet module install datadog-datadog_agent)
SaltStack: datadog-formula, applied as the 'datadog' state with the API key in pillar

flashcards.front: Agent v7 vs v6 vs v5
flashcards.back:
v7: current major version; runs Python 3 custom checks only.
v6: embeds Python 2 (optional Python 3 runtime from v6.14).
v5: legacy Python 2-based Agent.
Before moving from v6 to v7, verify custom checks are Python 3 compatible.

flashcards.front: Agent metrics vs cloud provider (crawler) metrics
flashcards.back:
Agent: collects every 15 seconds, 50+ metrics by default, plus integrations, logs, APM, processes and custom metrics.
Cloud providers: sample hosts externally every 5-25 minutes; AWS exposes per-minute metrics through its API.
Billing: an EC2 instance running the Agent and also found by the AWS integration is not billed twice.

flashcards.front: Agent v6/v7 architecture: main components
flashcards.back:
Main process: Collector (runs checks, collects metrics) + Forwarder (sends payloads to Datadog over HTTPS), with DogStatsD embedded.
Separate processes: APM/Trace Agent (enabled by default) and Process Agent (disabled by default except for container collection).

flashcards.front: Default Agent collection interval
flashcards.back: 15 seconds: the Collector gathers all standard metrics every 15 seconds.

flashcards.front: What does the Forwarder do when Datadog is unreachable?
flashcards.back: It buffers metrics in memory until a size or outstanding-request limit is reached; after that the oldest metrics are discarded to keep memory usage manageable.

flashcards.front: Linux Agent service commands
flashcards.back:
systemd: sudo systemctl start|stop|restart|status datadog-agent
Upstart (CentOS/RHEL 6, SUSE 11): swap 'systemctl <action>' for '<action>', e.g. sudo start datadog-agent
service wrapper: sudo service datadog-agent start|stop|restart

flashcards.front: Windows Agent service control
flashcards.back:
Service: DatadogAgent (display name 'Datadog Agent'), running as ddagentuser.
From an elevated prompt: "%ProgramFiles%\Datadog\Datadog Agent\bin\agent.exe" start-service | stopservice | restart-service (Windows-only subcommands).
Also: services.msc, Restart-Service -Force datadogagent (dependent services), or the Datadog Agent Manager.

flashcards.front: macOS Agent service control
flashcards.back:
launchd via launchctl:
Start: sudo launchctl kickstart system/com.datadoghq.agent
Stop: sudo launchctl kill SIGTERM system/com.datadoghq.agent
Restart: sudo launchctl kickstart -k system/com.datadoghq.agent
Status: sudo launchctl print system/com.datadoghq.agent (or the web GUI / systray app)

flashcards.front: Docker Agent lifecycle commands
flashcards.back:
Start/restart: re-run the docker run installation command (env vars are fixed at container creation)
Stop: docker exec -it <CONTAINER_NAME> agent stop
Status page: docker exec -it <CONTAINER_NAME> agent status

flashcards.front: Kubernetes Agent lifecycle commands
flashcards.back:
Stop/restart: kubectl delete pod <AGENT POD NAME> (the DaemonSet reschedules it automatically)
Status page: kubectl exec -it <POD_NAME> -- agent status

flashcards.front: Agent GUI (Datadog Agent Manager)
flashcards.back:
Launch: datadog-agent launch-gui (agent.exe launch-gui on Windows); opens http://127.0.0.1:5002.
Enabled by default on Windows and macOS, disabled on Linux; a GUI port of -1 disables it.
Localhost-only, needs browser cookies. Shows status, edits datadog.yaml and checks, shows logs, sends flares, restarts the Agent.

flashcards.front: Which OS user does the Agent run as?
flashcards.back:
Linux: dd-agent. Run checks as that user to match the service's permissions: sudo -u dd-agent -- datadog-agent check <CHECK_NAME>
Windows: ddagentuser (override with DDAGENTUSER_NAME at install).

flashcards.front: When must you restart the Agent?
flashcards.back: After changing datadog.yaml or an integration's configuration (conf.d/<INTEGRATION>.d/conf.yaml), so the Agent loads the change. Examples: sudo service datadog-agent restart (Ubuntu), sudo systemctl restart datadog-agent, agent.exe restart-service (Windows).

flashcards.front: systemctl status datadog-agent vs datadog-agent status
flashcards.back:
sudo systemctl status datadog-agent: whether the service is running, from systemd's view.
sudo datadog-agent status: the running Agent's status page (checks, forwarder, hostnames, errors).

flashcards.front: Agent hostname resolution order (first match wins)
flashcards.back:
1. Hostname set in the Agent config, unless it starts with ip- or domu
2. DNS/OS hostname, if it is not an EC2 default (e.g. ip-192-0-0-1)
3. EC2 instance ID, if the EC2 metadata endpoint is reachable
4. Fallback: DNS hostname, even if it is an EC2 default
Non-unique names such as localhost.localdomain are skipped.

flashcards.front: When does the Agent use the EC2 instance ID as the hostname?
flashcards.back: When no usable hostname is configured, the OS/DNS hostname is an EC2 default (ip-..., domu..., or EC2AMAZ-... on Windows with ec2_use_windows_prefix_detection), and the Agent can reach the EC2 metadata endpoint.

flashcards.front: hostname_fqdn
flashcards.back: datadog.yaml option (off by default) that makes Agent v6+ report the host's FQDN instead of the possibly short os.Hostname() result. Available on Linux/macOS since v6.3 and honored on Windows since v6.5; the MSI property HOSTNAME_FQDN_ENABLED (v6.20+) sets it at install.

flashcards.front: hostname_force_config_as_canonical
flashcards.back: When true (Agent 6.16+/7.16+), a configured hostname that starts with ip- or domu is accepted as the canonical hostname. When false (default), such a name is skipped and the Agent falls through to the EC2 instance ID.

flashcards.front: How do you see which hostname the Agent is using?
flashcards.back: sudo datadog-agent hostname prints the hostname in use; sudo datadog-agent status also lists the hostname candidates the Agent detected.

flashcards.front: Host aliases
flashcards.back: When one host has several unique names (instance ID, EC2 default name, DNS name), the Agent picks one canonical hostname and reports the others as aliases. Aliases appear in the Infrastructure List inspect panel but cannot be searched or filtered on.

flashcards.front: What happens when you change a host's hostname?
flashcards.back: The old hostname stays in the UI for two hours without new metrics; its data can still be queried through the API. Custom hostnames must follow RFC 1123 (letters, digits and hyphens).

flashcards.front: Duplicate hosts on AWS (e.g. EKS) and containerized hostname failures
flashcards.back:
Duplicates: the Agent cannot reach EC2 IMDS, so it sends no instance ID alias. Fix: allow IMDS access (hop limit 2 for containers) and use Agent 7.64.0+ or DD_EC2_PREFER_IMDSV2 for IMDSv2.
'Unable to reliably determine the host name': set DD_HOSTNAME on the Agent container.
